title: Endless halves: where does the total go?
hook: Keep adding half of what is left. Do the pieces ever add up to more than a whole?

knows: adding fractions with a common denominator
doesNotKnow: that infinitely many halves can add to a finite total

misconception: Adding infinitely many things must give infinity.
objective: The learner can explain that the halves 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + ... always fit inside a unit square, so their total cannot pass 1, and that it approaches exactly 1.

claims.text: After n terms, 1/2 + 1/4 + ... + 1/2^n = 1 − 1/2^n; after 6 terms that is 63/64, leaving a white sliver of 1/64.
claims.source: Geometric sum; recomputed in node for n = 6: 32/64 + 16/64 + 8/64 + 4/64 + 2/64 + 1/64 = 63/64. Stage prints (2^k - 1)/2^k from the same k that draws the pieces.

claims.text: Carried on forever, the total is exactly 1: the white sliver halves each time and shrinks toward nothing (the limit of 1 − 1/2^n).
claims.source: Limit of 1 - 2^-n as n grows is 1; the sum of an infinite series is defined as the limit of its partial sums.

claims.text: Every piece lies inside the unit square of area 1, so the total area of the pieces can never exceed 1.
claims.source: Each piece is half of the white region that remains, so the pieces never overlap and never leave the square (pieces() in Demo.tsx).

claims.text: Each step shades half of what is left, so the white part is halved every time and never reaches zero in finitely many steps.
claims.source: White after k steps is 1/2^k, which is positive for every finite k.

recall.question: You eat half a cake, then half of what is left, then half of that, and so on without end. How much cake do you eat in total?
recall.why: Each bite is half of what is left, so you never take more than the cake. The pieces add to 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + ... = 1, the whole cake.
